case_title: Sequence A — Incident, then public opinion binds, then hard regulation
question: Stage by stage, what follows from this ordering, what threat becomes live at each step, and what dated observable would show it?

ruling.ruling: Ordering runs in three stages: within 6-8 weeks the proximate-cause entity (developer or operator, whichever attribution names) announces a visible process/governance change while its model line keeps shipping unchanged; within the following 30-60 days formal state action (a licensing invocation against the operator, or liability language on an already-moving bill) lands, arriving after and distinct from the voluntary move; only after that formal action names the other party does it make an equivalent move, 8-16 weeks out and conditional, with symmetric or absent movement on both sides falsifying the whole sequence.
ruling.because: pressure-model's round-2 revision is the only minute that actually stages the question asked: it orders the proximate-cause entity's move ahead of the other party's, makes the second move conditional on and lagged behind the first, and gives an explicit falsifier (symmetric or null action). ai-public-backlash's round-2 revision supplies the second joint: voluntary lab/operator concession precedes formal state or regulatory action rather than following it. lab-moves supplies the third fact needed to complete the chain — the process-change announcement coexists with continued shipping, meaning the move is governance-layer, not capability-layer.
ruling.threat_live: Governance-layer announcements (a safety framework, an audit commitment, a review gate) become available as a substitute for capability-layer restraint — the model line keeps shipping — which is newly dangerous because it lets 'compliance visible cost' satisfy the political/legal pressure that ai-pressure and lab-moves describe without the underlying capability ever being curtailed; separately, per ai-regulation-teeth, rules with only disclosure power get cited as if they were the response but carry no enforcement, so the appearance of a regulatory stage can arrive without the stage's substance.
ruling.strongest_minute: pressure-model (v2.1, round 2) — it is the only minute that revised specifically to add sequencing (who moves first, how long the other party's move can lag, and under what condition) rather than just re-asserting a flat trigger window, and it names the exact falsification condition (symmetric or neither-moves) that a dated check can apply.
ruling.weakest_minute: ai-incident-severity — its round-2 DEFEND doubles down on 'rapid convergence onto joint liability standards' but supplies no dated, checkable observable for that convergence, which the question explicitly requires; declining to classify systemic-vs-one-off is honest, but the positive claim it does make is unfalsifiable as stated.
ruling.shared_assumption: That settled, quantified, public attribution mechanically produces a public, dated institutional response rather than quiet settlement, sealed litigation, or delayed non-public action — assumed by five of six minutes and engaged as an objection by only one (ai-pressure round 2, citing standard counsel advice to minimize public statements under live liability exposure).
ruling.smuggled_assumption: ai-regulation-teeth smuggles in that licensing/audit power attaches to the operator rather than the developer — a claim it flags itself in round 2 as 'bolted onto the mechanism, not derived from it' — and the brief grants only that attribution settles, not onto which of the two entities enforcement power specifically lands.
ruling.unresolved: Which entity is the proximate-cause first-mover — developer (ai-pressure, lab-moves), operator (ai-regulation-teeth), or both jointly (ai-incident-severity) — is not settled by the brief and the minutes argue past each other on it rather than resolving it; the staged sequence above is conditional on whichever entity attribution actually names, which the minutes cannot supply from a single incident.

ruling.ruling: Stage 1 (by ~2026-11-01): a governor/legislature invokes emergency or moratorium authority against a named deployment; Stage 2 (by 2026-11-12/15): a named lab pauses or reverses that deployment, with the live dispute being whether the announcement follows Stage 1 and cites the state action (ai-pressure) or precedes it and cites public sentiment only (lab-moves revised, ai-public-backlash); Stage 3 (by 2026-11-15): no party other than the lab holds a cost-imposing hook over reversal, so whatever posture results stays reversible at will (ai-regulation-teeth revised).
ruling.because: Four minutes converge on a lab pause/reversal landing in the 6-8 week window, but ai-public-backlash and lab-moves-revised are mutually exclusive on ORDER (state-first vs. lab-first) and ai-pressure vs. lab-moves-revised are mutually exclusive on CITED REASON (state opposition vs. public sentiment alone). ai-regulation-teeth's round-2 revision reframes the decisive question away from 'which move happens' to 'does anything binding attach to it,' and explicitly survives only if no governor's order lands with a violation-consequence -- which is exactly what ai-public-backlash's Stage 1 would supply if it fires.
ruling.threat_live: Binding opposition immediately triggers moves to un-bind it: ai-pressure's lab lobbies for federal preemption the moment it makes a voluntary concession, and ai-regulation-teeth argues no third party gets a cost-imposing hook regardless of which move happens -- so accountability's appearance (a pause, a safety board) arrives newly live at this stage without enforcement attached, which is a more dangerous state than either open defiance or a real rule, since it forecloses stricter follow-through while reading as responsiveness.
ruling.strongest_minute: ai-regulation-teeth (round 2 REVISE) -- it is the only minute that names a falsifiable discriminator (does a party other than the lab hold a cost if the lab reverts) rather than predicting which theatrical form the response takes, and it explicitly stakes itself against ai-public-backlash's moratorium scenario rather than ignoring it.
ruling.weakest_minute: pressure-model -- its claim resolves true under either 'doubles down publicly before 2026-11-12' or 'faces a second, larger reversal,' with the second branch given no date or size threshold, so the prediction cannot lose within the stated window.
ruling.shared_assumption: ai-pressure, lab-moves, ai-incident-severity, and pressure-model all assume the visible response to binding opposition takes the form of a single named lab's deployment pause/reversal by ~2026-11-12/15, without arguing why a deployment-level move (rather than, say, a pricing, access, or geographic change) is the mechanism binding opposition acts through.
ruling.smuggled_assumption: ai-incident-severity requires a SECOND, unrelated firm to make a comparable reversal within 60 days to classify the event as structural -- the brief grants only that opposition becomes binding once, not that it recurs across firms, so the second-mover condition is an assumption the minute introduces rather than one the brief supplies.
ruling.unresolved: Whether the lab's move or the state's move comes first, and whether the lab's stated reason is state/local political opposition or undifferentiated public sentiment -- the minutes split on both and none of the visible evidence in round 2 settles either ordering.

ruling.ruling: Stage 3's binding enforcement formalizes the lab's already-reversible Stage-2 posture into compliance paperwork without changing the targeted deployment, while producing a disclosed delay/scope-narrowing on some future release in the regulator's own jurisdiction — i.e., the specific deployment the moratorium hit stays reversible at the lab's discretion, but the regulator's forward-looking hook becomes the one lever in this chain a lab cannot simply outlast.
ruling.because: ai-regulation-teeth and lab-moves converge on a mechanism claim the others don't rebut: enforcement power is jurisdiction- and future-release-scoped, so it cannot retroactively lock in the Stage-1/2 deployment, and absent enforcement's already-passed target it becomes a cost absorbed into paperwork. ai-pressure and pressure-model add the one falsifiable delta this produces going forward — a disclosed delay/scope-narrowing tied explicitly to enforcement — which is a distinct, checkable claim rather than a rebuttal of the teeth argument, so both hold simultaneously about different objects (the old deployment vs. the next one).
ruling.threat_live: authority over frontier release timing partially migrates from unilateral lab discretion to a regulator with a pre-deployment blocking/disclosure hook — but only for releases still inside that regulator's forward reach; the deployment that triggered Stage 1 is explicitly named by the minutes as exempt from this new leverage, so the newly-live threat is narrower than 'regulation now binds labs' and is instead 'regulation now binds the *next* decision point.'
ruling.strongest_minute: ai-regulation-teeth — it's the only minute that states a falsifiable test for when regulation is theatre versus binding (does a named body hold pre-deployment block/delay plus disclosure power over *this specific* deployment), and it uses that test to correctly scope the claim rather than overgeneralizing to 'regulation now controls the lab.'
ruling.weakest_minute: ai-public-backlash — its claim is about press/optics framing rather than about what the ordering causally changes for the lab's decision, so it answers an adjacent question (how backlash is narrated) rather than what threat becomes live at Stage 3; it also concedes 'partial' grip without engaging the reversibility question at all.
ruling.shared_assumption: ai-pressure, lab-moves, and pressure-model all assume a binary decompose of lab response into either 'formalize into compliance paperwork, deployment unchanged' or 'visible delay/scope-narrowing' — none argues why some hybrid (e.g., silent quiet throttling with no disclosure, or delay for unrelated technical reasons misattributed to enforcement) is excluded; this is one shared framing, not three independent confirmations.
ruling.smuggled_assumption: ai-incident-severity's Stage-3 minute imports 'authority over frontier releases has shifted from unilateral lab discretion to an external body' as structural fact, but the brief only grants that a binding enforcement regime exists in one jurisdiction over one case — generalizing that to a structural authority shift is an assumption the ordering itself doesn't establish, and ai-regulation-teeth directly contests it.
ruling.unresolved: Whether the disclosed delay/scope-narrowing (if it happens) will be legally traceable to the enforcement action specifically, versus attributable to ordinary product timelines — none of the minutes specify how to distinguish genuine causal compliance from coincidental timing, which is exactly the ambiguity a lab's PR team would exploit.
